opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing R1 taught me is to pay attention to simplicity. Before that, many of us assumed reasoning ability would need very elaborate machinery: complex search, carefully designed process rewards, lots of human-annotated chains of thought. What we saw was that with a strong base model and a fairly clean reinforcement learning setup, with verifiable rewards and room for the model to explore, a lot of reasoning behavior just emerged. The model learned to reflect, to go back and check itself, to spend more tokens on harder problems. Nobody hand-wrote that.

So now, when I look at a new development, my first question is whether it's a genuinely scalable idea or a clever trick that works at one scale. I've become a bit skeptical of methods with too many hand-crafted components. If something gets better as you add more compute, more data, or more interaction with an environment, that excites me much more than a few points on a benchmark.

The second thing is that I now care a lot about the base model. R1 wasn't magic on top of nothing. The RL worked because the pretrained model already had latent capability, and RL drew it out. So I look at whether a new approach unlocks something already there or adds something new. Both matter, but they're different stories.

The third is openness. One of the most meaningful parts of that experience was seeing how fast the community built on it once the weights and methods were out. People reproduced it, found problems, and pushed it in directions we hadn't thought of. Progress is faster when ideas circulate. So I value work that is transparent about what worked and what didn't, because the failures are often the most useful part.

And honestly, it made me more humble about predictions. Things I thought were years away happened in months. So I try to stay curious, run the experiment, and let the model surprise me, rather than deciding in advance what it can't do.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. R1 changed how I look at things in a pretty concrete way, and I think the biggest lesson was about what you actually need versus what people assume you need.

Before R1, there was this widespread belief that strong reasoning had to come from large amounts of carefully labeled, step-by-step human data, with process reward models supervising every intermediate step. We went in a different direction. With R1-Zero especially, we found that if you give the model a verifiable signal, whether the final answer is right or wrong, and run reinforcement learning at scale, reasoning behaviors emerge on their own. Longer chains of thought, self-verification, backtracking, what people started calling the "aha moment." Nobody wrote those behaviors into the data. The model found them because they were useful for getting the reward.

So now, when I see a new development, the first question I ask is: what is the actual signal driving this? Is it something that scales, or is it dependent on human labor that will eventually bottleneck? I've become quite skeptical of approaches that rely on more and more handcrafted supervision. And I pay much more attention to anything that improves the quality or the breadth of verifiable feedback, because that's the lever that mattered most for us.

The second thing R1 taught me is about efficiency as a constraint rather than an afterthought. We didn't have unlimited compute, so every design decision had to justify itself. Honestly, that pressure made the research better. When I look at new work now, I'm less impressed by results that only come from throwing more resources at a problem, and more interested in ideas that change the slope. If a method gets a better result with the same compute, that's a real contribution. If it just gets a better result with ten times the compute, I'm not sure what we've learned.

And the third thing is a bit more philosophical. R1 made me more willing to trust simple ideas. The core recipe was not complicated. A good base model, a clear reward, a stable RL algorithm, and patience. A lot of the complexity people had been adding turned out to be unnecessary. So when something new comes along with a very elaborate pipeline, I ask whether the elaboration is actually load-bearing, or whether it's just there because nobody tried removing it.

The last point is that I became more humble about predicting what models will do. We expected improvement. We did not expect the specific behaviors that appeared. So I try to stay open to the idea that the next interesting thing may come from a direction that looks modest on paper. The important question is whether it has the right ingredients to let the model surprise you.

astra-6.text:
Working on R1 made me look more closely at how a model reaches an answer, rather than just how impressive the answer sounds. When I see a new development, I want to understand what actually improved: Can the model handle unfamiliar problems? Can it recognize a mistake and recover? Does the improvement hold up beyond a few carefully chosen examples?

It also made me more interested in simple ideas that scale. A complicated system can produce a striking demonstration, but I find it more exciting when a clear principle leads to consistent progress—and we can understand where it still breaks down.
